I'm going to assume this ignorant fatty has never had to cut into an obese person. Admittedly, neither have I, but I have had to assist in several surgeries on obese veterinary patients. I'll agree it's not identical, but it's very similar. As much as I agree that neither cats, dogs, nor obeasts are humans, they're all mammals, so they're all pretty similar on the inside. Well, except for the fat. Some of the surgeries I have assisted in have been for routine procedures (like a spay) and some have been for emergency situations (foreign body or bowel obstruction, for example).

Normal weight animals (and humans) have a small layer of subcutaneous fat ("under the skin" fat). On a routine abdominal procedure (like a spay), once you get past the skin & underlying fat, there's the abdominal wall. An incision is usually made into the linea alba (the "white line" that divides the left and right half of the abs) to minimize bleeding. All the organs are under the abdominal wall. Usually there is some fat in the abdominal cavity. This is visceral fat. This is the stuff that will kill you if you have too much of it.

I have participated in surgeries where there has been so much subcutaneous fat, that the vet has had to extend the incision or literally remove chunks of fat to reach the abdominal wall. This causes more bleeding and requires more sutures to close the incision, which results in the patient being under anesthesia longer. Obese patients are already a higher anesthetic risk than normies, so the longer they are under, the higher their chances of dying on the table become. Plus all this means a longer (and usually more painful) recovery period for the patient.

I still remember there was a spay surgery I had to assist with in which the patient (a dog, I think it was a beagle?) had so much visceral fat, the vet had to change his gloves THREE TIMES during surgery. The fat literally kept soaking the gloves and turning them translucent. I had never seen something like this before. It took quite a while, but the vet FINALLY found the uterus/ovaries under all that visceral fat. They were completely covered in fat, which is not normal for dogs. A surgery that normally takes 20-30 mins from first incision to the final suture took OVER AN HOUR because of all that fat.

All these experiences working with animals can easily be applied to "human" obeasts.

TL;DR: So it's not that doctors don't know how to operate on obeasts, it's that the surgery and anesthesia is much, much riskier due to their weight (even routine surgeries!) There's so much fat in the surgeon's way that it complicates the procedure, resulting in more time under anesthesia, longer incisions, more blood loss, more pain, and a longer recovery time.
